questiontext.text: What can Bellman-Ford do that Dijkstra cannot?

feedback.text: Correct — Bellman-Ford is designed for negative weights and can detect negative cycles.

answer.text: Run faster than Dijkstra on all graphs

feedback.text: The opposite — Bellman-Ford is slower; its value is generality.
MST is a different problem (Prim/Kruskal).

answer.text: Solve all-pairs shortest paths in one run

feedback.text: One run is single-source, like Dijkstra.

generalfeedback.text: Bellman-Ford trades speed for generality: it correctly handles negative edges and can report a negative cycle.

questiontext.text: In the standard Bellman-Ford algorithm, how many times is the full set of edges relaxed?

feedback.text: Correct — a shortest path has at most V-1 edges, so V-1 passes suffice.
Close, but V-1 passes are enough; a V-th pass is only used to detect negative cycles.
It relaxes all E edges per pass, but the number of passes is V-1.
That is not the Bellman-Ford bound.

generalfeedback.text: Because any shortest path uses at most V-1 edges, relaxing every edge V-1 times guarantees convergence.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of Bellman-Ford on V vertices and E edges?

feedback.text: Correct — V-1 passes, each relaxing all E edges.
That is Dijkstra with a binary heap.
That is Floyd-Warshall.
That resembles Kruskal's sorting cost, not Bellman-Ford.

generalfeedback.text: V-1 passes times E edges per pass gives O(V * E).

questiontext.text: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source?

answer.text: If one more relaxation pass still improves some distance, a negative cycle exists

feedback.text: Correct — distances should be final after V-1 passes; further improvement signals a negative cycle.

answer.text: If any distance becomes exactly zero

feedback.text: A zero distance is not evidence of a negative cycle.

answer.text: If the priority queue empties early

feedback.text: Bellman-Ford does not use a priority queue.

answer.text: If a vertex has no outgoing edges

feedback.text: A sink vertex says nothing about cycles.

generalfeedback.text: After V-1 passes all distances are final; running a V-th pass that still relaxes an edge proves a reachable negative cycle.

questiontext.text: Bellman-Ford correctly computes shortest paths on a graph with negative edge weights but no negative cycle.

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly the case it handles.
It does handle negative edges as long as no reachable negative cycle exists.

questiontext.text: On a graph with only non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford is generally faster than Dijkstra.

feedback.text: No — O(V*E) is typically slower than O((V+E) log V); prefer Dijkstra when weights are non-negative.
Correct — Bellman-Ford is slower; its advantage is handling negative weights, not speed.

questiontext.text: The main reason to choose Bellman-Ford over Dijkstra is support for ______-weight edges (one word, English term).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Bellman-Ford are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It can detect a negative-weight cycle

feedback.text: Yes — via an extra relaxation pass that still improves a distance.

answer.text: It relaxes every edge in each of V-1 passes

feedback.text: Yes — that is the core loop structure.

answer.text: It requires all edge weights to be non-negative

feedback.text: No — that requirement belongs to Dijkstra.

answer.text: It runs in O(V + E) time

feedback.text: No — it runs in O(V * E).

generalfeedback.text: Bellman-Ford: V-1 relaxation passes over all edges, O(V*E), handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.
